lead: A game engine is a software suite that turns models, textures, scripts and lights into a running VR or AR application. Unity and Unreal Engine are two common choices. Each gives an editor, a scene or level model, an asset pipeline, lighting tools, a scripting system and a build path to a headset or phone. The engine does not replace modelling or rendering theory; it packages those steps so a small team can assemble, test and ship an interactive 3D scene. This chapter compares their main objects and workflow, then shows how batching affects draw calls.
prereq: You need: Chapter 5.4 for scene graphs and Unit 4 for the rendering pipeline.

sections.h3: The engine as an editor and a scene model

blocks.text: A game engine is the workshop, not the theory. The editor is the authoring window where you place objects and set values. Unity organises a scene as a tree of GameObjects. A GameObject is a named object in the scene; it has no visible shape by itself. A Component is a block of data or behaviour attached to a GameObject. The Transform component stores position, rotation and scale. A Mesh Renderer component draws a mesh. A C# script component adds custom behaviour. A Prefab is a saved GameObject template that you can reuse across scenes. A Scene is one level or environment. The Asset Store is a marketplace of ready-made assets and tools. Unreal Engine uses a Level as the scene, an Actor as an object placed in it, and Components attached to the Actor. A Blueprint is a visual script graph; C++ is used for custom or performance-critical code. The editor runs the scene, updates components each frame, feeds input to scripts and sends draw commands to the GPU. A scene graph from Chapter 5.4 is the underlying idea; the engine adds editing, assets and build tools. Some syllabi call this game engine development.

An asset pipeline moves a model from a modelling tool into the engine. Export a mesh from Maya, 3ds Max or Blender, usually as FBX or glTF. A mesh is the object's geometry. Import it into the engine. The engine creates a mesh asset and a material slot list. A material is a shader plus values: base colour, roughness, metalness and textures. A shader is a small GPU program that computes surface shading. Shading decides how light reflects from the surface. Lighting can be real-time or baked. Baked lighting precomputes light falling on static objects and stores it in lightmaps; it is cheap at run time but does not move. Real-time lights update every frame and cost more. A camera projects the 3D scene to a 2D image. In perspective projection, distant objects look smaller and parallel lines meet at a vanishing point. In orthographic projection, parallel lines stay parallel and size does not fall with distance. VR uses two perspective cameras, one per eye, with a small eye separation to give stereo depth from two slightly different images. AR on a phone uses the rear camera image plus a virtual perspective camera matched to the phone camera. Build settings choose the target: a standalone headset, a PC-tethered headset or a phone. The build step compiles scripts, packs textures, selects the graphics API, the interface to the GPU, and produces an installable app.

sections.h3: Workflow and performance: draw calls and batching

blocks.text: Unity workflow: create a Scene, import assets, drag a Prefab into the Scene, attach C# scripts, set materials and lights, bake static lighting, then build. Unreal workflow: create a Level, place Actors, add Components, write Blueprint logic or C++, set materials and lights, build lighting, then package. Unity is often chosen for quick iteration, mobile AR and a large Asset Store. Unreal is often chosen for high-fidelity rendering and visual Blueprint prototyping. Both can target VR headsets through OpenXR, a cross-vendor XR API; for phones, AR is built with ARCore or ARKit (Unity AR Foundation, Unreal's ARCore/ARKit plugins). Performance is dominated by draw calls, fill rate and CPU work. Fill rate is pixels shaded per second. A draw call is one command from the CPU to the GPU to draw a mesh with a material and render state. Render state includes depth and blend settings. Batching combines meshes that share material and state into fewer draw calls. If a batch can hold at most B objects of one material, and nᵢ objects use material i, then:

blocks.where: Σ means sum over materials i; nᵢ is the number of objects with material i; B is the maximum objects per batch; ceil rounds up to a whole batch. Perfect batching means all objects with the same material fit into the fewest possible batches.

blocks.text: Perfect batching needs shared material and compatible render state. If materials differ, the engine must split batches. The worked example below applies this formula.

spec.aria: Three rows of 20 small squares, one row per material, each row bracketed into a group of 15 and a group of 5, each group labelled draw call.

examples.question: A Unity scene has 60 cubes in 3 materials, 20 cubes per material. A batch holds at most 15 cubes of one material. Find the number of draw calls with perfect batching and with no batching.
steps: Batches per material: ceil(20 ÷ 15) = ceil(1.333) = 2 batches.
Total batched draw calls: 3 materials × 2 batches per material = 6 draw calls.
With no batching, each cube needs its own draw call: 60 cubes × 1 draw call per cube = 60 draw calls.
examples.answer: With perfect batching the scene needs 6 draw calls, and with no batching it needs 60 draw calls.
examples.check:
import math
cubes = 60
materials = 3
per_material = cubes // materials
batch_capacity = 15
batched = materials * math.ceil(per_material / batch_capacity)
unbatched = cubes
print(batched)
print(unbatched)

traps: Draw calls are not one per object when batching works; batching needs a shared material and compatible render state.
Batch capacity applies per material, not to the whole scene: 20 cubes of one material with capacity 15 need 2 batches.
A GameObject or Actor is not the visible mesh; the mesh is an asset drawn by a renderer component.
Baked light is not live: baked lights do not move or change at run time.
Orthographic projection does not make far objects smaller; perspective projection does.

quiz.q: In Unity, what is a GameObject and what is a Prefab?
quiz.a: A GameObject is a named object in a scene that holds components; a Prefab is a saved GameObject template reused across scenes.

quiz.q: Why does batching reduce draw calls, and what must objects share?
quiz.a: Batching combines meshes into fewer GPU commands. Objects must share a material and compatible render state, such as depth and blend settings.

quiz.q: A scene has 45 cubes in 3 materials, 15 cubes per material. A batch holds at most 10 cubes of one material. Find draw calls with perfect batching and with no batching.
quiz.a: Per material: ceil(15 ÷ 10) = 2 batches. Total: 3 × 2 = 6 draw calls. No batching: 45 draw calls.

quiz.q: Two scenes have 60 cubes. Scene A has 10 materials with 6 cubes each. Scene B has 1 material with 60 cubes. A batch holds at most 15 cubes. Which scene has fewer draw calls? Show counts.
quiz.a: Scene A: 10 × ceil(6 ÷ 15) = 10 draw calls. Scene B: ceil(60 ÷ 15) = 4 draw calls. Scene B has fewer because its cubes share one material and batch into 4 groups.

quiz.q: In Unreal, what is an Actor and what is a Level?
quiz.a: An Actor is an object placed in the world; a Level is the scene or environment that contains Actors.

quiz.q: Why does VR use two perspective cameras rather than one orthographic camera?
quiz.a: Two perspective cameras, one per eye, give a slightly different view to each eye. That creates stereo depth; orthographic projection removes size falloff with distance and does not match normal stereo vision.

quiz.q: 60 cubes use 3 materials, 20 cubes per material. A batch holds at most 25 cubes of one material. Find draw calls with perfect batching and with no batching.
quiz.a: Per material: ceil(20 ÷ 25) = 1 batch. Total: 3 × 1 = 3 draw calls. No batching: 60 draw calls.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, Unity is common for mobile AR, standalone VR and rapid prototypes, while Unreal is common for high-fidelity VR training and visualisation. Modern engines expose OpenXR so one build can target several headsets, and render pipelines such as URP and HDRP, and Unreal features such as Lumen (global illumination) and Nanite (virtualised geometry), change the performance choices. Search next for Unity XR Interaction Toolkit, Unreal OpenXR, draw call batching and lightmap baking.
